sections.title: Transportation integration
paragraphs: 1 · Physics-constrained influence functions [S1] → trustworthy traffic state estimation. The advance (abstract level): measure how much each training example changes a constrained network model, while respecting the network's physical constraints (for example flow conservation at nodes). Problem it changes: when a traffic estimate looks wrong, agencies cannot tell which detector caused it; bad loops and stuck sensors silently distort corridor estimates. Mechanism: classic influence functions approximate the effect of removing one training point through a Hessian-weighted gradient; constraining that calculation to the feasible set (conservation, nonnegative densities) stops it from blaming or crediting physically impossible adjustments. Simplest credible test: a CTM-simulated freeway with 20 synthetic detectors; corrupt 2 (stuck-at-zero, +30% bias); fit a conservation-constrained estimator; rank detectors by influence. Baselines: leave-one-detector-out refitting (expensive but exact) and a simple residual-outlier rule. Metric: rank of the two corrupted detectors; agreement with leave-one-out. Effort: about 20 hours after the Residual Lab. What could make it fail: approximation breaks for highly nonlinear (congested) regimes; constraints not active where the fault is. Who cares: TMC operators, detector maintenance teams. Verdict: Try now, after the Residual Lab; it is the natural sequel to the verifier you are building.

2 · Signal control: max-pressure review [S3] and Traffic-VL [S2]. The advance: a consolidated view of max-pressure, a decentralized controller with a throughput-optimality result under its queueing assumptions, plus a vision-language controller that reportedly matches but does not beat a structured-state learner [S2], following earlier VLM controllers [S9]. Problem: adaptive control is expensive to deploy; agencies need methods that run on existing controllers with detector data they already have. Mechanism: max-pressure picks the phase with the largest sum of (upstream queue − downstream queue) weighted by saturation flow, so it reacts to spillback without a network model. Simplest credible test: a 4×4 grid in SUMO; compare fixed-time, actuated, max-pressure and an RL controller under normal demand and a lane-blocking incident; metric: average delay and throughput at saturation. Effort: about 15 hours once SUMO runs. What could make it fail: queue measurement error (max-pressure needs queues, most detectors give occupancy); RL overfits the training demand. Who cares: city signal engineers, controller vendors. Verdict: Try now as a learning project; Watch the VLM line, because a camera-to-signal model adds cost without a demonstrated gain over structured state.

One-liners: Crash Responder Safety Week [S4]: secondary crashes near incident scenes are a measurable safety problem, Watch for a small study once you have Florida crash data access. Robotaxi expansion and the Waymo–Uber change [S6][S7]: market structure news, no research action, Watch. Recalls meeting [S5]: no credible research link for you yet. Pathways to Safer Streets [S8] is April background, not new.

sections.title: Mentor calibration
paragraphs: P1 · MIT professor. Worldview update: influence functions give a falsifiable question, 'would removing this detector change the estimate?', which can be checked exactly by refitting [S1]. Terms: influence function; Hessian-vector product; leave-one-out; constrained optimization (KKT conditions); feasible set; throughput optimality; stability region. Belief vs last week: unchanged; insisting on exact checks (leave-one-out, relative gap) still holds [N1]. Deprioritize: interpreting influence scores without the leave-one-out check. Hard question: under what conditions does the first-order influence approximation fail, and how would you detect that on traffic data? Warning: three preprints read only at abstract level are not evidence you can build on yet.

P2 · Stanford PhD entrepreneur. Worldview update: detector health is a recurring, budgeted problem for every traffic management center; that is a more durable wedge than one grant cycle [S1]. Terms: TMC; detector health monitoring; maintenance work orders; data quality SLA; procurement through ITS maintenance contracts. Belief vs last week: shifted slightly from 'SS4A awardees first' toward 'TMC data quality first', because the buyer is recurring; still untested without interviews. Deprioritize: VLM signal products [S2]; each intersection needs cameras and compute. Hard question: what does a TMC currently spend to find and fix a bad detector? Warning: you have not done a single interview yet; both wedges are guesses.

P3 · OpenAI industry expert. Worldview update: Traffic-VL is an agent acting on infrastructure from pixels [S2]; the safety question is what checks sit between its output and the controller. Terms: action constraints; minimum green and pedestrian clearance as hard rules; fallback controller; monitoring; reward hacking in simulation; sim-to-real gap. Belief vs last week: unchanged that verification is the missing layer; extended from planning models to live control. Deprioritize: end-to-end controllers without a rule-based safety shell. Hard question: design a runtime monitor that would catch a learned controller starving a minor approach. Warning: reported wins over general VLMs say little about safety under rare events.

P4 · DeepSeek industry expert. Worldview update: a VLM matching a structured-state model [S2] means images bought generality claims, not performance; per intersection cost matters. Terms: edge inference; frames per second; model size vs latency; cost per intersection; max-pressure compute cost (near zero); quantization. Belief vs last week: reinforced, not revised: cheap structured models stay the deployable baseline [N1]. Deprioritize: GPU-at-every-intersection designs. Hard question: estimate the yearly cost of running a VLM controller at 300 intersections versus max-pressure on existing controllers. Warning: matching a baseline is not beating it; check that compute budgets were equal.

P5 · Transportation systems practitioner. Worldview update: max-pressure is the academic method closest to what agencies can actually run [S3]; detector quality decides whether it works. Terms: actuated control; coordination; detector occupancy vs queue length; NTCIP; ATC controllers; MUTCD pedestrian clearance; Traffic Incident Management. Belief vs last week: unchanged. Deprioritize: methods that need queue lengths measured by cameras the agency does not own. Hard question: max-pressure needs queues, but most signals report occupancy; how would you estimate queues from what exists? Warning: never compare a new controller only to fixed-time; compare to well-tuned actuated control.

Synthesis. Agreements: all five want a classical baseline (actuated control, max-pressure, leave-one-out) and an exact check. Disagreement: P2 now leans toward TMC data quality as a business, while P1 and P5 see it first as a research question with a clear test; they agree the next step is the same simulation. P3 and P4 agree on deprioritizing camera-to-signal models but for different reasons (safety vs cost). Open questions: can influence scores find bad detectors reliably? How should queues be estimated from occupancy for max-pressure?
